A.title: Shinjuku Ni-chōme: Tokyo’s Gay District, Without the Guidebook Filler
A.body:
--- title: 'Shinjuku Ni-chōme: Tokyo’s Gay District, Without the Guidebook Filler' description: 'Ni-chōme is the densest concentration of gay bars in the world — roughly 300 venues in a few blocks. How it became Tokyo’s gay district, how the bars actually work (bottle keep, scene specialization), and what a visitor should know.' pubDate: 'Aug 10 2026' updatedDate: 'Aug 10 2026' heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/shinjuku-nichome-guide.jpg' tags: ['Shinjuku', 'Ni-chome', 'Gay Tokyo', 'Bar Districts', 'Nightlife'] category: 'Bars' keyword: 'nichome tokyo' faq: - question: 'What is Shinjuku Ni-chōme?' answer: 'Ni-chōme (新宿二丁目) is a district of Shinjuku, Tokyo, and the densest gay neighborhood in the world. Within about five blocks centered on Naka-dōri, an estimated 300 gay bars and nightclubs operate, alongside restaurants, saunas, love hotels and cruising spaces.' - question: 'How did Ni-chōme become a gay district?' answer: 'It began in the American occupation era and accelerated after the 1956 Anti-Prostitution Law closed the area’s licensed red-light districts. As the traditional sex industry left, a gay subculture took its place, with gay bars publicly operating there from the late 1950s.' - question: 'How do Ni-chōme bars work?' answer: 'Most bars seat fewer than a dozen customers and are specialized by "scene" — bear, BDSM, young men, butch-femme lesbians, and more. Patrons sit at a counter and talk with the bartender; karaoke is popular, and a bottle-keep system is common, where regulars store their own bottle at the bar.' - question: 'Are Ni-chōme bars welcoming to foreign visitors?' answer: 'Most bar owners accommodate new and non-Japanese customers, but the scene is built around Japanese regulars and some venues discourage or prohibit foreigners regardless of language ability. The bars with foreigner-friendly reputations are well known; going in blind is hit-or-miss.' - question: 'What events happen in Ni-chōme?' answer: 'Rainbow Reel Tokyo (the film festival formerly the Tokyo International Lesbian & Gay Film Festival, founded 1992) and Tokyo Rainbow Pride, whose parade draws thousands and usually runs from Shibuya through Harajuku to Yoyogi Park.' --- Tokyo has one of the largest gay neighborhoods in the world, and almost nobody writing about Tokyo nightlife in English mentions it. **Shinjuku Ni-chōme** sits a ten-minute walk from the neon of Kabukicho, in the same ward, and packs an estimated **300 gay bars and clubs into a few blocks** — the highest concentration on the planet. This guide is the practical version: how the district came to be, how the bars actually work (because they do not work like a Western gay bar), and what a visitor should know before walking in. If you are looking for specific first-visit bars, our [Shinjuku niche bars guide](/blog/shinjuku-niche-bars/) lists the established foreigner-friendly venues by name; this one explains the district itself.
What this guide covers
  • Why Ni-chōme exists — the red-light-district history
  • How the bar scene is organized, including the bottle-keep system
  • The scene specialization that makes every bar different
  • What a foreign visitor should expect, honestly
## Where it is Ni-chōme is **Area 2 of the Shinjuku district** (the part of Shinjuku ward, not the station). It is a short walk from three stations: **Shinjuku San-chōme Station**, **Shinjuku Gyoenmae Station**, and **Shinjuku Station** itself. The core of the scene is the five blocks around **Naka-dōri**, between the BYGS building at Shinjuku San-chōme and a small park three blocks east. That puts it five to ten minutes from the Kabukicho nightlife covered in our [Kabukicho guide](/blog/kabukicho-tokyo-guide/), which makes the two districts easy to combine in one night — and easy to confuse, which matters, because the atmospheres could not be more different. ## How it became the gay district The history is the opposite of accidental. Ni-chōme's gay scene grew directly out of the collapse of the area's licensed red-light districts. In the American occupation era (1945–1952), a gay scene began forming, and a gay tea shop is documented as early as **1948**. By the 1950s gay bars were operating in Ni-chōme by name. Then came the **Anti-Prostitution Law of 1956** — the law that made paid sex illegal in Japan for the first time and ended the *akasen* (licensed red-light) system. As the traditional sex industry left Ni-chōme, the gay subculture that had been forming quietly took over the space. The district then accumulated the landmarks of Japan's LGBT history: a counseling room for young gay men in **1976**, the first AIDS candlelight vigil in **1986**, the **Tokyo International Lesbian & Gay Film Festival** in **1992** (now Rainbow Reel Tokyo), and Japan's **first lesbian and gay pride parade in 1994**. One more recent note worth knowing: in **2012** the national "no dancing" rule was enforced in several Ni-chōme clubs — the same law that shaped Tokyo's club scene — and was lifted in **2014**. The district's dance clubs now operate freely. ## How the bars actually work The single most important fact about Ni-chōme is that it is not one scene. It is hundreds of tiny scenes. Most Ni-chōme bars **seat fewer than a dozen customers**, and each is deliberately specialized — the district is organized by what the owners call "scene." There are bars for the **bear community**, for **BDSM**, for muscular men, for young men, for **butch-femme lesbians**, and every other niche you can name. In a society where many LGBT Japanese kept their sexuality private, these specialty bars provided the anonymity and the specificity that a general bar could not. The experience in most venues is counter service: you sit, talk with the bartender, and possibly sing. Two conventions matter: - **Bottle keep (ボトルキープ).** Regulars store their own bottle of liquor at the bar, which is why so many customers keep returning to one place. It is also how the loyalty that funds bar-organized outings — to onsen, hanami parties, picnics — is built. - **Karaoke.** Almost everywhere, and the most reliable icebreaker in the district. ## What a visitor should expect The honest version, because the guidebook version oversells it: - **Most bar owners accommodate new and non-Japanese customers.** You will not be turned away from the district, and the popular foreigner-friendly bars are established and known. - **But the scene is built around Japanese regulars, and some venues discourage or prohibit foreigners** regardless of Japanese ability. This is not hostility; it is the anonymity system doing its job. Do not take it personally, and do not push. - **The bars worth going to blind are the ones with an established foreigner-friendly reputation.** Picking a random door in Ni-chōme is genuinely hit-or-miss in a way that is not true of Kabukicho's mainstream venues. For anyone visiting Japan and looking for the gay scene, the practical pairing is Ni-chōme for the bar district and [Tokyo Rainbow Pride](/blog/shibuya-clubs-guide/) season (usually spring) for the community-scale events. ## The events Two annual events anchor the district: - **Rainbow Reel Tokyo** — the film festival, founded in 1992 and one of the oldest of its kind in Asia. - **Tokyo Rainbow Pride** — the pride parade and festival, which typically draws several thousand people and runs from Shibuya Station through Harajuku and Omotesandō to Yoyogi Park. Both are the occasions when the district's small bars host events too big for their own rooms, and the whole neighborhood fills with people who are not regulars. If you want to see Ni-chōme at full strength, that is the week. ## The bottom line Ni-chōme is Tokyo's gay district and the densest gay bar scene in the world, with a history tied directly to the end of Japan's licensed red-light districts. It is worth a night — ideally in combination with Kabukicho, ten minutes away, and ideally in one of the district's established foreigner-friendly venues rather than a random door. Come with cash, sit at the counter, and let the bartender set the tone. **Photo:** Shinjuku Ni-chōme, October 2019 by LittleT889, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shinjuku_Ni-ch%C5%8Dme.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0. **Sources:** [Wikipedia — Shinjuku Ni-chōme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku_Ni-ch%C5%8Dme); [Japan Times — Shinjuku gay enclave in decline but not on the surface](http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/nn20100224f1.html); [VICE — Japan lifts its "no dancing" law](https://www.vice.com/en/article/after-a-long-legal-battle-japan-finally-lifts-its-notorious-no-dancing-law/). Facts only; venue counts and pricing change, so confirm before you go.

B.title: Shinjuku Nightlife: Choose by Area, Purpose and Last Train
B.body:
---
title: 'Shinjuku Nightlife: Choose by Area, Purpose and Last Train'
description: 'Decide where to go in Shinjuku at night by purpose, first-visit fit and whether you need the last train. Compare Kabukicho, Golden Gai, Omoide Yokocho, Ni-chome and Nishi-Shinjuku without a fixed club ranking.'
pubDate: 'Nov 20 2025'
heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/shinjuku-nightlife-guide.jpg'
tags: ['Shinjuku', 'Nightlife', 'Bars', 'Golden Gai']
category: 'Area Guides'
keyword: 'shinjuku nightlife'
updatedDate: 'Oct 05 2026'
faq:
  - question: "Which part of Shinjuku should I visit at night?"
    answer: "Choose by the evening you want, not by a fixed club list. Omoide Yokocho is a compact dining alley by Shinjuku Station’s west side. Golden Gai is small individual bars near the east exit. Kabukicho is the larger entertainment district beside it. Shinjuku Ni-chome is the LGBTQ+ bar district a short walk away. Nishi-Shinjuku is the west-side option for hotel-area dining and a quieter skyline view. Check the venue’s own hours before you go."
  - question: "Where are the nightclubs in Shinjuku?"
    answer: "GO TOKYO places large entertainment venues, including a live venue and club, in Kabukicho and Tokyu Kabukicho Tower, and names Shinjuku as one of Tokyo’s late nightlife areas. There is no single official club ranking or shared admission price. Use the venue’s own event page for the date, age rule and charge, and do not follow a street tout."
  - question: "What time is the last train from Shinjuku?"
    answer: "There is no one last-train time. GO TOKYO says Tokyo trains generally stop around midnight and restart around 5 or 6 a.m. JR East’s Shinjuku timetable and Tokyo Metro’s last-train search are the sources for a specific line, direction and date. Check that departure before the evening, and plan a taxi or a stay-out if you will still be in Kabukicho, Golden Gai or Ni-chome after it."
  - question: "How can I avoid trouble when choosing a bar in Kabukicho?"
    answer: "Do not accept a street tout’s offer. Check a venue’s menu and charges before ordering. The Tokyo Metropolitan Police English page for visitors explains tout-related trouble and lists how to contact police. This guide does not claim any street or venue is safe."
---

Shinjuku nightlife is several different nights within walking distance of one station. The useful choice is not “best club” but which area matches the evening you actually want, whether a first visit can walk in, and whether you must be back at a ticket gate before the trains stop. [GO TOKYO’s nightlife overview](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/see-and-do/nightlife/index.html) describes Shinjuku as busy until dawn, from Golden Gai’s tiny bars to Kabukicho’s larger entertainment, and says trains generally stop around midnight.

Checked 5 October 2026 against GO TOKYO, JR East and Tokyo Metropolitan Police pages linked below. Hours, cover charges, last trains and which bars welcome walk-ins change by venue and date. This page does not keep a club ranking or a price table.

## Choose an area

| If you want… | Start with… | First-visit fit | Last-train constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dinner in a very small alley before a longer night | Omoide Yokocho, west of Shinjuku Station | Easy to find the alley; seats are only about five or six per stall, so a group may split. GO TOKYO lists cash. | About 2 minutes on foot from Shinjuku Station, so it is the easiest stop to leave for a train. Hours vary; confirm the stall. |
| A drink in a tiny, individual bar | Golden Gai, a few minutes from the east exit | Some bars welcome walk-ins and some are members-only. Many open relatively late, typically around 20:00. Seating is often five or six. | Leave earlier than the timetable: GO TOKYO’s walking time from Shinjuku Station is about 5 minutes, longer in a crowd. |
| A club, live venue, cinema or large entertainment venue | Kabukicho, beside Golden Gai | Tokyu Kabukicho Tower contains a hotel, cinema, theater, live venue and club, each with its own schedule. Street offers are not a venue list. | Same east-exit side as Golden Gai. A late event can outlast the trains; decide the return before you enter. |
| LGBTQ+ bars and clubs | Shinjuku Ni-chome | A dense bar district, not a single venue. House rules, cover and who is welcomed vary by bar. | Shinjuku-sanchome is the closer station for some exits. Use the line’s own last train, not a district average. |
| A quieter meal or night view on the west side | Nishi-Shinjuku | Hotel and office towers rather than a bar alley. Useful when the plan is dinner or a view, not bar-hopping. | West exit of Shinjuku Station. Still confirm the venue; a view restaurant is not an all-night area. |

These are separate stops. Golden Gai and Kabukicho sit on the east side; Omoide Yokocho and much of Nishi-Shinjuku are west of the station. Do not treat a walk between them as one continuous venue.

Official area notes, checked 5 October 2026:

- [Shinjuku Golden Gai on GO TOKYO](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/spot/62/index.html): about 280 bars in six lanes, some members-only, hours vary, no smoking or drinking in the street, no photography without permission. Updated 27 November 2025.
- [Omoide Yokocho on GO TOKYO](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/spot/63/index.html): a tiny yakitori alley about 2 minutes from Shinjuku Station, cash listed, hours and prices to be confirmed with the stall. Updated 27 November 2025.
- [Tokyu Kabukicho Tower on GO TOKYO](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/spot/1855/index.html): hotel, cinema, theater, live venue and club in one complex; each facility sets its own schedule.
- [GO TOKYO nightlife](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/see-and-do/nightlife/index.html): trains stop around midnight and start again around 5 or 6 a.m.; taxis are the practical late ride. Updated 13 August 2026.

Ni-chome and individual west-side restaurants are not given a shared official hours page. Use the venue site, and use the district guides below for how those areas differ.

## Last train, or stay out

Pick this before the second stop.

1. **You need a specific train.** Open [JR East’s Shinjuku timetable](https://timetables.jreast.co.jp/en/timetable/list0866.html) for JR lines, or Tokyo Metro’s last-train search for Metro lines. The time depends on line, direction and whether the day is a weekday. GO TOKYO’s “around midnight” is an area warning, not your departure.
2. **You can miss it.** Staying out is a real option in Kabukicho and Ni-chome, not a failure of the plan. Budget a taxi back, or wait for the first trains after about 5 a.m. Do not assume a bar will remain open until then.
3. **Walk time counts.** Omoide Yokocho is the short walk to the west side of Shinjuku Station. Golden Gai and Kabukicho need the east-exit walk GO TOKYO estimates at about 5 minutes before crowds. Leave earlier than the printed departure.

Club and live-venue nights fail when the event time and the train time are planned separately. If the venue has not published that night’s hours, it is not yet a plan.

## Three routes that stay checkable

These are sequences, not reservations. Confirm each place on the day.

**Dinner, then one small bar, then the train.** Start at Omoide Yokocho while seats exist, cross to Golden Gai only if a bar is open to walk-ins, and return to Shinjuku Station for the train you already looked up. Read the [Golden Gai guide](/blog/golden-gai-shinjuku-guide/) for lane rules before you go; this page does not repeat them.

**A venue night in Kabukicho.** Choose one published event at a named venue, such as a live show or club night inside Tokyu Kabukicho Tower, from that venue’s own page. Ignore street offers on the way in. The [Kabukicho guide](/blog/kabukicho-tokyo-guide/) covers how to read the district; this page does not rank clubs or copy admission fees.

**Ni-chome, with an explicit stay-or-leave choice.** Go for the bar district itself, not as an add-on after several other areas. The [Ni-chome guide](/blog/shinjuku-nichome-guide/) explains how those bars differ. If the last train from Shinjuku-sanchome or Shinjuku is already close, treat the visit as a first stop another night. For a jazz bar or other niche room rather than the district, use the [Shinjuku niche-bars guide](/blog/shinjuku-niche-bars/).

## Practical and safety notes

Golden Gai is also a place where people live and work. GO TOKYO asks visitors not to smoke or drink in its streets and says photography needs permission.

In Kabukicho, a street tout may offer a deal. Do not follow one. Read the menu and charges before ordering. The Tokyo Metropolitan Police explain impersonation scams, street solicitation and how to get help on their [English page for visitors](https://www.keishicho.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/multilingual/english/safe_society/victim_of_crime/ninpo.html). Nothing here is a safety guarantee.

Entry rules, cover charges and menus belong to each business. If a figure is not on that business’s current page, this guide does not supply one.

**Photo:** Kabukicho's red gate at night by Basile Morin, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kabukicho_red_gate_and_colorful_neon_street_signs_at_night,_Shinjuku,_Tokyo,_Japan.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

A.title: Asakusa at Night: Sensoji, the Streets, and the Quiet Side of Tokyo After Dark
A.body: --- title: 'Asakusa at Night: Sensoji, the Streets, and the Quiet Side of Tokyo After Dark' description: 'Asakusa is a daytime landmark, but its night is real: Sensoji lit up, Nakamise quiet, and a handful of old bars and restaurants along the river. What stays open, what it costs, and why it is worth one late evening.' pubDate: 'Aug 10 2026' updatedDate: 'Aug 10 2026' heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/asakusa-night.jpg' tags: ['Asakusa', 'Tokyo', 'Sensoji', 'Nightlife', 'Bars', 'Japan Travel'] category: 'Area Guides' keyword: 'sensoji night' faq: - question: 'Is Asakusa lively at night?' answer: 'It is quieter than Shinjuku or Shibuya, but not dead. Sensoji itself is lit and walkable after dark, Nakamise shuts its shutters, and the streets around the station and along the river keep a handful of old bars and restaurants open until about midnight.' - question: 'Can you enter Sensoji at night?' answer: 'The temple grounds are open and walkable at night, and the pagoda and main hall are lit. The hall itself closes in the early evening, but the precincts remain accessible and are far less crowded after dark.' - question: 'What does Asakusa nightlife cost?' answer: 'The old drinking bars around Asakusa run 1,000-3,000 yen per drink at the simple end, and a meal at a classic restaurant along the river is 3,000-8,000 yen. It is cheaper and less pressured than central Tokyo nightlife.' - question: 'Are Asakusa bars foreigner-friendly?' answer: 'The newer bars and the izakaya near the station generally are. Some of the oldest mom-and-pop drinking bars are old-fashioned and cash-only with no menu, but they are used to curious visitors - cash, a translation app and a smile go far.' - question: 'What is the last train from Asakusa?' answer: 'The Asakusa and Ginza subway lines run until roughly midnight, and the Tsukuba Express a little later. After that, taxis are the option; the area is north-east of central Tokyo, so a taxi to Shinjuku is long and expensive.' --- import { Image } from 'astro:assets'; import asakusaNight from '../../assets/heroes/asakusa-night.jpg'; Asakusa is on every Tokyo itinerary for the daytime: the Sensoji temple, the Nakamise shopping street, the rickshaw rides. Almost nobody writes about the night, which is exactly why it is worth one. The honest version is that Asakusa after dark is the opposite of Shinjuku. It is quiet, old, and mostly shuttered by midnight. But what stays open is genuinely different from anywhere else in Tokyo - a handful of decades-old bars and restaurants on streets that have not changed much since the 1960s. ## What stays open **Sensoji itself.** The temple grounds are open and walkable at night, with the pagoda and the main hall lit until late. The main hall closes in the early evening, but the precincts - the huge lantern, the approach - remain accessible and are dramatically less crowded than the daytime crush. This alone is worth the trip. **Nakamise.** The shopping street that runs to the temple shuts its shutters by early evening. The character of the approach changes entirely; instead of a tourist gauntlet, it becomes a quiet, lantern-lit path. Strolling it after dark is one of the simplest pleasures in the area. **The drinking streets.** Asakusa has a genuine old drinking culture that most visitors never see. Look for the small bars and izakaya on the side streets off the main approach and along the Kaminarimon-dori - mom-and-pop places that have been running for decades. The Rokku district, a block or two south-east of the temple, is the historical entertainment quarter and holds several of these. **The river.** The Sumida riverbank, a few minutes' walk west of the temple, has a strip of restaurants and bars with views of the river and the Asahi building. In summer, the outdoor seating is one of the better spots in Tokyo for a drink near water. ## What it costs Asakusa is cheaper than central Tokyo's nightlife. | Item | Typical | |---|---| | Drink at a simple bar | 1,000-3,000 yen | | Izakaya evening with food | 3,000-6,000 yen | | Riverfront restaurant meal | 3,000-8,000 yen | The old bars are mostly cash-only, and many have no written menu. As with the [old bars in Osaka](/blog/osaka-local-nightlife/), the protocol is cash, a translation app, and pointing at what looks good. ## Practical notes **Getting there and back.** Asakusa is on the Asakusa and Ginza subway lines, and the Tsukuba Express. Last trains run until roughly midnight; after that, taxis are the option, and a taxi to central Tokyo is long and expensive. Plan the return before the last round. **Foreigner-friendliness.** The newer bars and the izakaya near the station are comfortable with visitors. The oldest places are old-fashioned and cash-only, but they are used to curious tourists and the barrier is language, not policy. A smile and a bad attempt at Japanese go a long way. **Combining it.** Asakusa is north-east of the main nightlife districts, so it does not naturally combine with a Shinjuku or [Shibuya night](/blog/shibuya-clubs-guide/). Treat it as its own evening - ideally an early one that ends before midnight - rather than a stop on a crawl. ## The bottom line Asakusa's night is not the Tokyo that party guides describe. It is quieter, older, cheaper, and mostly closed by midnight. That is precisely its value: a Sensoji precinct lit and nearly empty, a Nakamise with the shutters down, and a few genuinely old bars that have not changed in fifty years. If you want one evening that feels like the Tokyo of an earlier era, this is it. **Photo:** Senso-ji @ Asakusa at night by Guilhem Vellut, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Senso-ji_%40_Asakusa_at_night_(9821706664).jpg), CC BY 2.0. **Sources:** [Wikipedia - Sensoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sens%C5%8D-ji); [Wikipedia - Asakusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asakusa). District layout and general practice; prices are the working range and always confirm before ordering.

B.title: Kyoto Nightlife: What Actually Happens After Dark in the Old Capital
B.body: --- title: 'Kyoto Nightlife: What Actually Happens After Dark in the Old Capital' description: 'Kyoto closes early by Tokyo standards, and the nightlife that exists is concentrated — Gion, Pontocho, Kiyamachi, and a few bar streets near the station. Where to go, what it costs, and what a visitor should expect.' pubDate: 'Aug 10 2026' updatedDate: 'Aug 10 2026' heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/gion-night.jpg' tags: ['Kyoto', 'Kyoto Nightlife', 'Gion', 'Pontocho', 'Bars', 'Japan Travel'] category: 'Area Guides' keyword: 'kyoto nightlife' faq: - question: 'Is there nightlife in Kyoto?' answer: 'Yes, but it is concentrated and it closes earlier than Tokyo. The main districts are Gion, Pontocho, Kiyamachi and the areas around Kyoto Station. Most bars wind down by 1 AM, and the traditional geisha districts are quiet by any standard.' - question: 'Where do locals go out in Kyoto?' answer: 'Kiyamachi is the riverfront strip of bars and restaurants, Pontocho is the narrow alley of upscale dining and small bars, and Gion holds the traditional and high-end venues. Around Kyoto Station there are newer, more casual bars.' - question: 'How much does a night out in Kyoto cost?' answer: 'A casual bar or izakaya evening runs ¥3,000–¥6,000 per person. Pontocho restaurants and Gion ryotei are a different bracket — ¥10,000–¥30,000 or more. As in Osaka, the smaller the bar, the more likely it is cash-only.' - question: 'Do Kyoto bars welcome foreign visitors?' answer: 'The casual bars around Kiyamachi and the station generally do. Gion is more guarded: many ryotei and ochaya work by introduction and do not admit walk-ins, and the area has signs asking visitors not to chase geisha on the street.' - question: 'What is the last train in Kyoto?' answer: 'The subway runs until roughly midnight; JR lines run a little later. After that, taxis are the realistic option. Kyoto is compact, so a taxi across the city is short but not cheap at night.' --- import { Image } from 'astro:assets'; import gionNight from '../../assets/heroes/gion-night.jpg'; Kyoto is the city that everyone visits for the daytime temples and nobody writes honestly about the night. The honest version: **Kyoto's nightlife exists, it is concentrated in a few districts, and it closes early by Tokyo standards.** That is not a flaw; it is the character of the place, and knowing it in advance is the entire difference between a good night and a confused one. ## Where Kyoto's night actually is Four districts carry almost the whole thing. **Gion.** The city's most famous night district, in the sense that the geisha districts are part of it. The Hanamikoji and Shirakawa streets are lined with ryotei (traditional restaurants) and ochaya (teahouses), many of which work by introduction and do not admit walk-ins. Walking through at night is beautiful and free; getting seated at an ochaya is not something a visitor can usually just do. The area has posted signs asking tourists not to chase or touch geisha on the street, and the request should be taken seriously. **Pontocho.** A single narrow alley between Kamo River and the main street, about a five-minute walk from Gion. It is dense with restaurants and small bars, several with river-view terraces in summer. More of it is open to walk-ins than Gion, but the upscale end is reservation territory. This is the best single street in Kyoto for a memorable dinner with a bar afterward. **Kiyamachi.** The riverfront strip running north of Shijo, a few blocks west of Pontocho. This is where the casual scene lives: izakaya, bars, standing bars, small clubs. It is the closest thing Kyoto has to a "going out" street, and the most foreigner-accessible of the four. **Around Kyoto Station.** A newer, more scattered scene of casual bars and izakaya, useful if you are staying near the station and want a low-effort night. Not a destination on its own. ## What it costs The usual two-bracket structure applies, the same as [Osaka](/blog/osaka-local-nightlife/). | Bracket | What | Typical spend | |---|---|---| | Casual | Kiyamachi izakaya and bars | ¥3,000–¥6,000 | | Mid | Pontocho restaurant with drinks | ¥8,000–¥15,000 | | High | Gion ryotei / ochaya | ¥20,000+ (often by introduction) | The small bars in Kiyamachi are mostly cash-only and rarely post menus — the same convention as the [Tenma and Kyobashi bars in Osaka](/blog/osaka-local-nightlife/), and the same solution: cash, a translation app, and pointing at what looks good. ## The geisha question Worth addressing directly, because it is what most visitors actually wonder about. **You are unlikely to see a geisha on the street by waiting, and you cannot simply book an ochaya as a walk-in.** The modern reality is that most geisha work is arranged through regular customers, and the entertainment is expensive and formal. What a visitor can reasonably do: - Walk Gion and Pontocho at night for the atmosphere — that is the real spectacle - Attend a public cultural performance, if the timing aligns - Skip the street-chasing behaviour entirely There is no legitimate "geisha experience" that involves approaching performers on the street, and the area's signs exist because the problem got bad enough to need them. ## Practical notes **Closing times.** Kyoto winds down earlier than Tokyo. Most casual bars are done by midnight to 1 AM; the street scene is quiet by 1:30. The subway runs until roughly midnight, JR a little later. **Taxis.** After the trains stop, taxis are the realistic option. Kyoto is compact — a taxi across the central area is short — but night fares add up, and the supply around the bar districts thins late. **Etiquette.** The one rule that matters in Gion: do not block the narrow alleys, do not chase performers, and do not enter an ochaya uninvited. In Kiyamachi the usual bar rules apply — shower before anything serious, cash in an envelope, no photos inside a small bar. **Combining with the rest of the trip.** Kyoto pairs naturally with the [Osaka local nightlife guide](/blog/osaka-local-nightlife/), since Osaka is thirty minutes by train and stays open later. A common pattern is Kyoto by day, Osaka for the late night — the two cities are different halves of one region. ## The bottom line Kyoto's night is not Tokyo's, and it is not supposed to be. It is concentrated in Gion, Pontocho and Kiyamachi, it closes early, and its most famous venues work by introduction. Go for the atmosphere of the old streets, eat well in Pontocho, drink casually in Kiyamachi, and take the geisha question off the table. That is a genuinely good Kyoto night. **Photo:** Gion at night by Adrián Pérez, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gion_at_Night_(26895328445).jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0. **Sources:** [Wikipedia — Gion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gion); [Wikipedia — Pontochō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontoch%C5%8D); [Wikipedia — Kiyamachi](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/木屋町通). District layout and general practice; prices are the working range and always confirm before ordering.

A.title: Yui Tenma (天馬ゆい): The Voice-Actor Hopeful Who Retired, Returned, and Writes Tokusatsu Scripts
A.body:
---
title: 'Yui Tenma (天馬ゆい): The Voice-Actor Hopeful Who Retired, Returned, and Writes Tokusatsu Scripts'
description: 'Japanese AV actress Yui Tenma — debuted 2018 as "Sora Kamikawa," retired 2020, returned as Yui Tenma in 2021, and built a career that now includes writing tokusatsu scripts and appearing on Netflix. A voice-acting trainee whose career went sideways and then wide.'
pubDate: 'Aug 10 2026'
updatedDate: 'Aug 10 2026'
heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/tenma-yui.webp'
tags: ['Yui Tenma', 'AV Actress', 'JAV', 'Adult Film', 'Tokusatsu']
category: 'JAV Actresses'
keyword: 'yui tenma av actress'
faq:
  - question: 'When did Yui Tenma debut in AV?'
    answer: 'Twice. First in April 2018 as Sora Kamikawa, then — after retiring in June 2020 — again as Yui Tenma in 2021, with her first title under the new name released in June 2021.'
  - question: 'Why did she enter the industry?'
    answer: 'She had trained at a voice-acting school, drawn by anime, and applied on her own to an actress recruitment. Her background was the otaku-culture entry.'
  - question: 'What makes her career unusual?'
    answer: 'She writes tokusatsu (special-effects) scripts — she has written all four episodes of a 2025 series — and has appeared on Netflix, in indie film, and on radio, all while active in AV.'
  - question: 'What are her rankings?'
    answer: '#1 on the FANZA streaming weekly in June 2025; #9 in the monthly ranking for September 2025; and top 10s in March and May 2026.'
  - question: 'Is she still active?'
    answer: 'Yes, as of 2026, across many studios, with a 100-plus title count by her own 2024 count.'
---

import SnsEmbed from '../../components/SnsEmbed.astro';

Yui Tenma's career is the voice-acting dream gone sideways, then gone wide. **A trainee at a voice-acting school who applied to the AV industry on her own, debuted in 2018, retired in 2020, returned under a new name in 2021 — and now writes tokusatsu scripts, appears on Netflix, and still works in AV.** The second career is not an escape from the first; it is running alongside it.

## The short version

| | |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Yui Tenma (天馬ゆい) · formerly Sora Kamikawa (上川星空) |
| **Born** | 14 February 1998, Aomori |
| **Debut 1** | April 2018, MOODYZ, as Sora Kamikawa |
| **Retired 1** | June 2020 |
| **Debut 2** | 2021, as Yui Tenma |
| **Titles** | 100+ (2024) |
| **Also** | Tokusatsu actress and scriptwriter; Netflix; indie film |

## 2018–2020: Sora Kamikawa, the first run

She grew up anime-obsessed, trained at a **voice-acting school**, and applied to the industry on her own. Her first run, as **Sora Kamikawa**, began in **April 2018** on MOODYZ and ended in **June 2020** with retirement.

## 2021: the return as Yui Tenma

On **18 March 2021** she announced the return under **Yui Tenma**. Her first title under the new name released in June 2021. She has worked freelance across many studios — MOODYZ, Alice Japan, Fitch, Max-A and others — and by her own 2024 count had passed **100 titles**.

The 2022 Alice Japan title *Girls' Track Club Member* sold roughly 10,000 copies in a week, and its re-discovery drove a **#2 FANZA streaming weekly in September 2023**.

## The tokusatsu and mainstream track

The non-AV work is where the voice-acting training surfaced:

- **2021–** — villainess role in GIGA's tokusatsu series *Wakusei Sentai WAKUSAIBER* (SEASON 2 in 2022, *Kaijū Sentai Jūkaizā* in 2022)
- **2025** — **scriptwriter for all four episodes** of *Sōdō Sentai Gōkengō*, on top of acting
- **2023** — indie film *Onmitsu Nuremochichō*
- **2025** — **Netflix's Death Kiss Game** (resident role)
- **2022** — entry in the DMM GAMES voice-acting audition for *Crimson Youma Taisen*

## Rankings

- **June 2025** — **#1, FANZA streaming weekly**
- **September 2025** — #9, FANZA monthly
- **March 2026 / May 2026** — #10, FANZA monthly

## Now

Active in AV as of 2026, with regular event work — including an appearance at the TRE expo in Taipei in 2024 — and the tokusatsu writing continuing. Her X account documents the day-to-day, including her event schedule.

<SnsEmbed
	kind="x"
	url="https://x.com/tenma_yui2/status/2078921230422560896"
	label="Yui Tenma (@tenma_yui2) on X — the event schedule"
/>

## What this career means

**The voice-acting training that did not go to waste — it went sideways.** Tenma's original aim, acting, became the AV career, and then the acting re-surfaced in the industry's most literal form: writing and performing tokusatsu. The retire-and-return shape is [the same as Amatsuki's](/blog/amatsuki-azu/); the tokusatsu scriptwriting is what makes hers distinct. It is the industry's most otaku-native career on this site.

## Related reading

- [JAV actresses: how the career actually works](/blog/jav-actresses-explained/) — retirement and return
- [Azu Amatsuki](/blog/amatsuki-azu/) — the other two-name return
- [Jun Kasui](/blog/kasui-jun/) — another career with a second track
- [How Japan's adult video industry works](/blog/japanese-adult-video-industry/) — MOODYZ and Alice Japan

**Sources:** [Japanese Wikipedia — 天馬ゆい](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/天馬ゆい). Career facts only; nothing here is sourced from fan wikis or aggregator biographies.

A.title: Saori Hara (原紗央莉): The AV Actress Who Disappeared in 2011 and Returned as Someone Else
A.body:
---
title: 'Saori Hara (原紗央莉): The AV Actress Who Disappeared in 2011 and Returned as Someone Else'
description: 'AV actress Saori Hara — junior idol, SOD exclusive from 2008, a debut reported at 100,000-plus sales, Best Actress 2010, then gone after March 2011 and back in 2014 under a new name. The documented record.'
pubDate: 'Aug 10 2026'
updatedDate: 'Aug 10 2026'
heroImage: '../../assets/heroes/saori-hara.webp'
tags: ['Saori Hara', 'AV Actress', 'JAV', 'Adult Film', 'Retirement']
category: 'JAV Actresses'
keyword: 'saori hara'
faq:
  - question: 'When did Saori Hara debut in AV?'
    answer: 'She signed an exclusive contract with Soft On Demand (SOD) in September 2008 and debuted in January 2009. Her debut title was reported to have sold over 100,000 copies.'
  - question: 'What did she do before AV?'
    answer: 'She was a junior idol under the name Mai Nanami from around 2004, singing the theme for the TV Osaka anime Marshmallow Communication and appearing in television and film, before re-emerging as Saori Hara in 2008.'
  - question: 'When and why did she leave the industry?'
    answer: 'In March 2011, after the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, she suffered a nervous breakdown and decided to leave the entertainment industry, cancelling her SOD contract. She announced her retirement in August 2011.'
  - question: 'Did she ever return?'
    answer: 'Yes. In February 2014 she announced her return to entertainment under the name Matsunoi Miyabi, with no intention of returning to the AV industry. She appeared in nude gravure in April 2014 and later in the GARO tokusatsu series.'
  - question: 'What awards did she win?'
    answer: 'Best Actress at the 2010 Sky PerfecTV! Adult Broadcasting Awards, for her work in 2009.'
---

Saori Hara's career is the industry's version of a disappearing act with a sequel. **A junior idol who signed with SOD in 2008, debuted in January 2009 to reported sales over 100,000, won the 2010 Adult Broadcasting Award — and then, in March 2011, after the Tohoku earthquake, vanished.** She came back in 2014 under a different name, and the AV industry never saw her again.

## The short version

| | |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Saori Hara (原紗央莉) · later Matsunoi Miyabi (松野井雅) |
| **Born** | 1 January 1988, Hiroshima |
| **Before AV** | Junior idol "Mai Nanami," from 2004 |
| **AV debut** | January 2009, Soft On Demand (contract from September 2008) |
| **Award** | Best Actress, Adult Broadcasting Awards 2010 |
| **Left** | March 2011 (announced retirement August 2011) |
| **Returned** | February 2014 as Matsunoi Miyabi |
| **Now** | Actress (GARO series) |

## The junior idol years

She began as a junior idol under the name **Mai Nanami** (七海まい) around **2004**, singing the theme song for the TV Osaka anime *Marshmallow Communication* and appearing in a TBS drama and a film. It was a conventional child-entertainment start.

In **2008** she re-emerged as **Saori Hara** — gravure DVD in August, first nude in the magazine *Sabra* in September, and the announcement of an exclusive contract with **Soft On Demand** (SOD) that same month.

## 2009: the SOD debut

She made her AV debut in **January 2009** with SOD. Her debut title was reported to have sold **more than 100,000 copies** — an exceptional number for a debut, driven by the crossover from her idol years.

She stayed exclusive to SOD for the entire AV career, with no label moves. In **March 2010** she won **Best Actress at the Sky PerfecTV! Adult Broadcasting Awards** for her 2009 work.

## 2011: the disappearance

In **March 2011**, immediately after the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, she suffered a nervous breakdown and decided to leave the entertainment industry entirely, cancelling her SOD contract. Her final original AV title was released in May 2011, and she formally announced her retirement in **August 2011**.

The details of the breakdown are her own; the relevant public record is that the departure was not a contract ending but a person leaving, abruptly, after a national disaster.

## 2014: the rebirth

In **February 2014** she announced her return to entertainment under the name **Matsunoi Miyabi** (松野井雅), explicitly stating that she had no intention of returning to the AV industry. In **April 2014** she appeared in nude gravure in *Weekly Playboy* under the title "Rebirth."

From 2015 she appeared in the tokusatsu series *GARO -GOLDSTORM-* as the character Amiri, and she continued to work in mainstream television and film.

## What the career means

**A debut that was a headline, and an exit that was a disappearance.** The junior-idol crossover made her debut a 100,000-sale event; the 2011 departure made her exit the kind of story the industry remembers. And the 2014 return, under a new name and explicitly outside the AV industry, is the rarest of the exits on this site — the one where the performer walked away and stayed away, into a different entertainment career.

Against the site's other profiles — [Yoshizawa writing her own record](/blog/akiho-yoshizawa/), [Okita withdrawing her catalogue](/blog/anri-okita/) — Hara's is the career that simply left the building and built a second one next door.

## Related reading

- [JAV actresses: how the career actually works](/blog/jav-actresses-explained/) — debut routes and retirement
- [How Japan's adult video industry works](/blog/japanese-adult-video-industry/) — SOD and the studio structure
- [Yuma Asami](/blog/yuma-asami/) — an exit shaped by illness
- [Sora Aoi](/blog/sora-aoi/) — the crossover template

**Sources:** [English Wikipedia — Saori Hara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saori_Hara). Career facts only; nothing here is sourced from fan wikis or aggregator biographies.
